I. $\displaystyle \int_0^1 t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt$

II. $\displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{t^{z}}{te^t} \, \textrm dt$

III. $\displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{e^t}{t^{1-z}} \, \textrm dt$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad \textrm{Re}(z) > 0.
$$

With this definition in mind, let's consider each of the given integrals.

- Integral I does *not* match the definition. The upper bound of integration does not match that given in the definition.

- Integral II matches the definition:

$$
\int_0^\infty \dfrac{t^{z}}{te^t} \, \textrm dt = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t} \, \textrm dt = \Gamma(z)
$$

- Integral III does *not* match the definition. The integrand $\dfrac{e^t}{t^{1-z}}$ is not equivalent to that shown in the definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172064 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-58e93e99-d92a-5ce1-a5e1-f2a7ff45e177" "question-cb5b08f1-b473-53d8-ae61-be733c058e2d" "question-8f3249d6-edac-5050-9528-d13b2bdbb793" "question-d0d87553-dab1-5046-8598-8f79d15fc0d7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186171870 :question/problem "Evaluate $\Gamma(7).$" :question/worked-solution "For any natural number $n \geq 1,$ we have

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\Gamma(7) = 6! = 720.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172065 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bd01511b-f45a-5cd4-b173-d099f3266062" "question-6bbc8ec2-1cd6-5115-ab81-c2fbacd13746" "question-38540fee-f0e4-596e-9eff-9715fa0a19af" "question-0fdfcf02-67ae-5263-baa1-a6ba5d9b1b6d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186171871 :question/problem "Calculate $\Gamma \left( \dfrac{5}{2} \right).$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(\frac{5}{2}) & =\frac{3}{2}Γ(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-0d9f5142-140d-5b22-b957-299741979b12" :question/id #uuid "0d9f5142-140d-5b22-b957-299741979b12" :question/math-academy-id "q-107888" :question/problem "Which of the following integrals are equivalent to $Γ(z)$ for $\text{Re}(z)>0?$

I. ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t$

II. ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{t}^{z-1}}{{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t$

III. ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the definition of the gamma function:

$$
Γ(z)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t,\,\text{Re}(z)>0.
$$

With this definition in mind, let's consider each of the given integrals.

- Integral I matches the definition:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t=Γ(z)
$$

- Integral II matches the definition:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{t}^{z-1}}{{e}^{t}}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t=Γ(z)
$$

- Integral III does *not* match the definition. The lower bound of integration does not match that given in the definition.

:question/problem "Which of the following integrals are equivalent to $Γ(z)$ for $\text{Re}(z)>0?$

III. $3{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{t}^{3z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the definition of the gamma function:

$$
Γ(z)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t,\,\text{Re}(z)>0.
$$

With this definition in mind, let's consider each of the given integrals.

- Integral I matches the definition. We use a substitution $s={t}^{3},$ then $3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t=\text{d}s.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{3z-1}{e}^{-{t}^{3}}\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{3(z-1)+2}{e}^{-{t}^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{3(z-1)}{e}^{-{t}^{3}}(3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{s}^{z-1}{e}^{-s}\,\text{d}s=Γ(z).\end{aligned}
$$

- Integral II does *not* match the definition. The integrand ${t}^{3z-3}{e}^{-{t}^{3}}$ is not equivalent to that shown in the definition.

- Integral III does *not* match the definition. The lower bound of integration does not match that given in the definition.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9a6b14e4-15be-5db4-bf56-15f3f68a2ded"] :db/ensure Therefore,

In particular, for any natural number $n \geq 1,$ we have

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!
$$

If the complex number $z$ satisfies $\textrm{Re}(z) > 0,$ then the gamma function can be defined as the improper integral

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt.
$$

In this lesson, we will only consider cases where $z$ is a positive real number." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173180 :tutorial/content "To evaluate the gamma function at positive integer multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

We'll prove these results at the end of the lesson." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173224 :tutorial/content "Here, we'll prove the recursive formula for the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

The formula comes from applying integration by parts to the integral in the definition of the gamma function. By definition,

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad\textrm{Re}(z) > 0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(z+1) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{z}{e}^{-t}{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }-z{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }(-\frac{{t}^{z}}{{e}^{t}})-{(-\frac{{t}^{z}}{{e}^{t}})|}_{t=0}+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }z{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =0-0+z{{{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t}_{⏟}}_{Γ(z)} \\  & =zΓ(z)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173181 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the following relationship between the gamma function and the factorial:

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!
$$

This relationship holds for any natural number $n \geq 1.$ Now, let's prove it.

First, we start with the following identity, which we proved earlier:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

For any natural number $n \geq 1,$ the above identity states the following:

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n \Gamma(n)
$$

Now, let's repeatedly expand out the right-hand side, noticing that most of the terms can be grouped into a factorial:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(n+1) & =nΓ(n) \\  & =n\cdot \overset{Γ(n)}{\overset{⏞}{(n-1)\cdot Γ(n-1)}} \\  & =n\cdot (n-1)\cdot \overset{Γ(n-1)}{\overset{⏞}{(n-2)\cdot Γ(n-2)}} \\  & =… \\  & ={{n\cdot (n-1)\cdot (n-2)\cdot …\cdot 1}_{⏟}}_{n!}\cdot Γ(1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n! \cdot \Gamma(1).
$$

To evaluate $\Gamma(1),$ we can use the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} \, \textrm dt = 1
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n!
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173182 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the fact that $\Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}.$ To prove this, we can directly compute the value of $\Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)$ using the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t
$$

We simplify this integral using the substitution $t = u^2,$ which implies $\text{d}t = 2u \, \text{d}u.$ Also, note that $u \to 0^+$ as $t \to 0^+$ and $u \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ So, we have

$$
t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = (u^2)^{-1/2} e^{-u^2} \cdot 2u \, \text{d}u = e^{-u^2} \cdot 2 \, \text{d}u.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = 2 \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u.
$$

This is directly related to the well-known **Gaussian integral**:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

Since the integrand $e^{-u^2}$ is even (i.e., symmetric about the $y$-axis), we have

$$
\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi}.
$$

Substituting this result back into our expression for the Gamma function, we obtain

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi} = \sqrt{\pi}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172142 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

In particular, for any natural number $n \geq 1,$ we have

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!
$$

If the complex number $z$ satisfies $\textrm{Re}(z) > 0,$ then the gamma function can be defined as the improper integral

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt.
$$

In this lesson, we will only consider cases where $z$ is a positive real number." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173180 :tutorial/content "To evaluate the gamma function at positive integer multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

We'll prove these results at the end of the lesson." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173224 :tutorial/content "Here, we'll prove the recursive formula for the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

The formula comes from applying integration by parts to the integral in the definition of the gamma function. By definition,

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad\textrm{Re}(z) > 0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(z+1) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{z}{e}^{-t}{|}_{0}^{\infty }-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }-z{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{t\to \infty }(-\frac{{t}^{z}}{{e}^{t}})-{(-\frac{{t}^{z}}{{e}^{t}})|}_{t=0}+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }z{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =0-0+z{{{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t}_{⏟}}_{Γ(z)} \\  & =zΓ(z)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173181 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the following relationship between the gamma function and the factorial:

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!
$$

This relationship holds for any natural number $n \geq 1.$ Now, let's prove it.

First, we start with the following identity, which we proved earlier:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

For any natural number $n \geq 1,$ the above identity states the following:

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n \Gamma(n)
$$

Now, let's repeatedly expand out the right-hand side, noticing that most of the terms can be grouped into a factorial:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(n+1) & =nΓ(n) \\  & =n\cdot \overset{Γ(n)}{\overset{⏞}{(n-1)\cdot Γ(n-1)}} \\  & =n\cdot (n-1)\cdot \overset{Γ(n-1)}{\overset{⏞}{(n-2)\cdot Γ(n-2)}} \\  & =… \\  & ={{n\cdot (n-1)\cdot (n-2)\cdot …\cdot 1}_{⏟}}_{n!}\cdot Γ(1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n! \cdot \Gamma(1).
$$

To evaluate $\Gamma(1),$ we can use the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} \, \textrm dt = 1
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n!
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173182 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the fact that $\Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}.$ To prove this, we can directly compute the value of $\Gamma \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)$ using the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t
$$

We simplify this integral using the substitution $t = u^2,$ which implies $\text{d}t = 2u \, \text{d}u.$ Also, note that $u \to 0^+$ as $t \to 0^+$ and $u \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ So, we have

$$
t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = (u^2)^{-1/2} e^{-u^2} \cdot 2u \, \text{d}u = e^{-u^2} \cdot 2 \, \text{d}u.
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = 2 \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u.
$$

This is directly related to the well-known **Gaussian integral**:

$$

$$

["question-8aae46a7-7405-5484-9202-26c3555ea95d" :question/math-academy-id "q-107832"] ["question-8aae46a7-7405-5484-9202-26c3555ea95d" :question/problem "Which of the following integrals are equivalent to $Γ(z)$ for $\text{Re}(z)>0?$

I. ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{e}^{t}}{{t}^{z-1}}\,\text{d}t$

II. ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{t}^{z}}{t{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t$

III. ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t$"] ["question-8aae46a7-7405-5484-9202-26c3555ea95d" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the definition of the gamma function:

$$
Γ(z)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t,\,\text{Re}(z)>0.
$$

With this definition in mind, let's consider each of the given integrals.

- Integral I does *not* match the definition. The integrand $\frac{{e}^{t}}{{t}^{z-1}}$ is not equivalent to that shown in the definition.

- Integral II matches the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{t}^{z}}{t{e}^{t}}\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t=Γ(z)\end{aligned}
$$

- Integral III matches the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{t}^{z-1}{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t=Γ(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-8aae46a7-7405-5484-9202-26c3555ea95d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ(\frac{7}{2}) & =\frac{5}{2}\,Γ(\frac{5}{2}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,Γ(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{\pi } \\  & =\frac{15}{8}\sqrt{\pi }\end{aligned}

One-Half"}] :question/problem "Calculate $\Gamma \left(\dfrac{5}{2} \right)$." :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the gamma function at multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

So, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Γ(\frac{5}{2}) &= \frac{3}{2}Γ(\frac{3}{2}) \\
&= \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}Γ(\frac{1}{2}) \\
&= \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{π} \\
&= \frac{3}{4}\sqrt{π}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050380} {:db/id 17592186172231 :question/id #uuid "985175a0-3817-5f02-8236-9b18519858f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-105737" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172065 2. $\displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{t^{z}}{te^t} \, \textrm dt$
3. $\displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{e^t}{t^{1-z}} \, \textrm dt$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's recall the definition of the gamma function:

- Integral III does *not* match the definition. The integrand $\dfrac{e^t}{t^{1-z}}$ is not equivalent to that shown in the definition.

[{:db/id 17592186172946 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173179 :tutorial/content "The **gamma function** $\Gamma(z)$ extends the factorial function to positive real numbers and parts of the complex plane.

In particular, for any natural number

$$
n \geq 1
$$

we have

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)
$$

If the complex number $z$ satisfies $\textrm{Re}(z) > 0$, then the gamma function can be defined as the improper integral

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt
$$

In this lesson, we will only consider cases where $z$ is a positive real number." :tutorial/id #uuid "9fea375f-e55b-5c47-a7ae-c2ef9f860a2c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5337 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "4bee0881-4e23-5850-9acc-e043caf9668c" :step/math-academy-id 33407 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172952}} {:db/id 17592186172947 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172064 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171870 :question/id #uuid "62da71f1-5a3a-509a-a68e-0596f88c4ae4" :question/math-academy-id "e-8951"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "59f9abf1-17db-5717-8660-a531ef00b15c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049341}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172230} {:db/id 17592186172234}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Gamma Function for a Positive Integer"} :step/id #uuid "96bce02d-680a-5dd7-a5f2-34c1e5553c65" :step/math-academy-id 33409 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172948}} {:db/id 17592186172948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173180 :tutorial/content "To evaluate the gamma function at positive integer multiples of one-half, we use the following recursive formula:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z), \qquad \Gamma \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

We'll prove these results at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "a2e308ea-2921-5cda-bb43-b4914e8efaf1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5338 :tutorial/title "The Recursive Formula and the Value of the Gamma Function at One-Half"} :step/id #uuid "5e5c30dd-3fe8-5761-b1e6-76ab3ced125d" :step/math-academy-id 33410 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172949}} {:db/id 17592186172949 :step/content {:db/id 17592186172065 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171871 :question/id #uuid "5d084f86-9874-5bdd-a416-dba742d7e4e5" :question/math-academy-id "e-8952"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4c8de43f-dc61-5bbe-8b84-b8aa0be19146" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050380}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186172231} {:db/id 17592186172235}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Gamma Function at a Multiple of One-Half"} :step/id #uuid "bf112a76-b1a6-5da1-b844-9eb0f13eb3f1" :step/math-academy-id 33411 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173037}} {:db/id 17592186172950 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173181 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the following relationship between the gamma function and the factorial:

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)
$$

This relationship holds for any natural number

$$
n \geq 1
$$

Now, let's prove it.

First, we start with the following identity, which we proved earlier:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

For any natural number

$$
n \geq 1
$$

the above identity states the following:

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n \Gamma(n)
$$

Now, let's repeatedly expand out the right-hand side, noticing that most of the terms can be grouped into a factorial:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Γ(n + 1) &= nΓ(n) \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot Γ(n - 1)^(⏞)^(Γ(n)) \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdot Γ(n - 2)^(⏞)^(Γ(n - 1)) \\
&= … \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdot … \cdot 1_(⏟)_(n!) \cdot Γ(1)
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n! \cdot \Gamma(1)
$$

To evaluate $\Gamma(1)$, we can use the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} \, \textrm dt = 1
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "66ce2df9-01d6-5873-b9e6-bb9e2a7d35af" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5339 :tutorial/title "Proving the Relationship Between the Gamma Function and the Factorial"} :step/id #uuid "272794b0-bed3-5ee3-a248-3dc313b1fd31" :step/math-academy-id 33412 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172951}} {:db/id 17592186172951 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173182 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the fact that

$$
\Gamma \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

To prove this, we can directly compute the value of

$$
\Gamma \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right)
$$

using the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t
$$

We simplify this integral using the substitution $t = u^2$, which implies

$$
\text{d}t = 2u \, \text{d}u
$$

Also, note that $u \to 0^+$ as $t \to 0^+$ and $u \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$. So, we have

$$
t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = (u^2)^{-1/2} e^{-u^2} \cdot 2u \, \text{d}u = e^{-u^2} \cdot 2 \, \text{d}u
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = 2 \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u
$$

This is directly related to the well-known **Gaussian integral**:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

Since the integrand $e^{-u^2}$ is even (i.e., symmetric about the $y$-axis), we have

$$
\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi}
$$

Substituting this result back into our expression for the Gamma function, we obtain

$$

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

The formula comes from applying integration by parts to the integral in the definition of the gamma function. By definition,

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad\textrm{Re}(z) > 0
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
Γ(z + 1) &= \int_{0}^{∞}t^{z}e^{-t}dt \\
&= \left.- t^{z}e^{-t}\right|_{0}^{∞} - \int_{0}^{∞} - zt^{z - 1}e^{-t}dt \\
&= lim_(t → ∞)(-\frac{t^{z}}{e^{t}}) - \left.(-\frac{t^{z}}{e^{t}})\right|_{t = 0} + \int_{0}^{∞}zt^{z - 1}e^{-t}dt \\
&= 0 - 0 + z\int_{0}^{∞}t^{z - 1}e^{-t}dt_(⏟)_(Γ(z)) \\
&= zΓ(z)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68b4463b-d790-5bf1-9972-da35d3818a8b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6699 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Recursive Formula"} :step/id #uuid "b3e9fad8-09f6-5769-9d53-ab348d94359e" :step/math-academy-id 40566 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172950}}] :activity/title "The Gamma Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172142} {:db/id 17592186172946 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173179 :tutorial/content "The **gamma function** $\Gamma(z)$ extends the factorial function to positive real numbers and parts of the complex plane.

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

The formula comes from applying integration by parts to the integral in the definition of the gamma function. By definition,

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1} e^{-t} \, \textrm dt, \qquad\textrm{Re}(z) > 0
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
Γ(z + 1) &= \int_{0}^{∞}t^{z}e^{-t}dt \\
&= \left.- t^{z}e^{-t}\right|_{0}^{∞} - \int_{0}^{∞} - zt^{z - 1}e^{-t}dt \\
&= lim_(t → ∞)(-\frac{t^{z}}{e^{t}}) - \left.(-\frac{t^{z}}{e^{t}})\right|_{t = 0} + \int_{0}^{∞}zt^{z - 1}e^{-t}dt \\
&= 0 - 0 + z\int_{0}^{∞}t^{z - 1}e^{-t}dt_(⏟)_(Γ(z)) \\
&= zΓ(z)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68b4463b-d790-5bf1-9972-da35d3818a8b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6699 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Recursive Formula"} :step/id #uuid "b3e9fad8-09f6-5769-9d53-ab348d94359e" :step/math-academy-id 40566 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172950}} {:db/id 17592186172950 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173181 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the following relationship between the gamma function and the factorial:

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)
$$

This relationship holds for any natural number

$$
n \geq 1
$$

Now, let's prove it.

First, we start with the following identity, which we proved earlier:

$$
\Gamma(z+1) = z \Gamma(z)
$$

For any natural number

$$
n \geq 1
$$

the above identity states the following:

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n \Gamma(n)
$$

Now, let's repeatedly expand out the right-hand side, noticing that most of the terms can be grouped into a factorial:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Γ(n + 1) &= nΓ(n) \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot Γ(n - 1)^(⏞)^(Γ(n)) \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdot Γ(n - 2)^(⏞)^(Γ(n - 1)) \\
&= … \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdot … \cdot 1_(⏟)_(n!) \cdot Γ(1)
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n! \cdot \Gamma(1)
$$

To evaluate $\Gamma(1)$, we can use the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} \, \textrm dt = 1
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Gamma(n+1) = n
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "66ce2df9-01d6-5873-b9e6-bb9e2a7d35af" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5339 :tutorial/title "Proving the Relationship Between the Gamma Function and the Factorial"} :step/id #uuid "272794b0-bed3-5ee3-a248-3dc313b1fd31" :step/math-academy-id 33412 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172951}} {:db/id 17592186173181 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the following relationship between the gamma function and the factorial:

$$

$$

$$

the above identity states the following:

$$

$$

Now, let's repeatedly expand out the right-hand side, noticing that most of the terms can be grouped into a factorial:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Γ(n + 1) &= nΓ(n) \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot Γ(n - 1)^(⏞)^(Γ(n)) \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdot Γ(n - 2)^(⏞)^(Γ(n - 1)) \\
&= … \\
&= n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdot … \cdot 1_(⏟)_(n!) \cdot Γ(1)
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$

To evaluate $\Gamma(1)$, we can use the definition of the gamma function:

Therefore,

$$
\Gamma \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

To prove this, we can directly compute the value of

$$
\Gamma \left(\dfrac{1}{2} \right)
$$

using the definition of the gamma function:

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t
$$

We simplify this integral using the substitution $t = u^2$, which implies

$$
\text{d}t = 2u \, \text{d}u
$$

Also, note that $u \to 0^+$ as $t \to 0^+$ and $u \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$. So, we have

$$
t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = (u^2)^{-1/2} e^{-u^2} \cdot 2u \, \text{d}u = e^{-u^2} \cdot 2 \, \text{d}u
$$

Thus, we get

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t} \, \text{d}t = 2 \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u
$$

This is directly related to the well-known **Gaussian integral**:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

Since the integrand $e^{-u^2}$ is even (i.e., symmetric about the $y$-axis), we have

$$
\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2} \, \text{d}u = \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi}
$$

Substituting this result back into our expression for the Gamma function, we obtain

$$
\Gamma\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \sqrt{\pi} = \sqrt{\pi}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "79026717-bbea-524a-a1e0-01ef7570bfac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5340 :tutorial/title "Evaluating the Gamma Function at One-Half"} :step/id #uuid "7a3ab1f8-c83c-5b32-87fd-ef21fb859957" :step/math-academy-id 33413} {:db/id 17592186173182 :tutorial/content "Previously, we used the fact that

17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.
On completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
